host.guideLocalDoorRequired: Serving works when ohmail opens your own mailbox on this computer. It stays off while this install mirrors a hosted account.

host.guideListenerPending: Nearly there — the engine is opening its door for your devices.

host.guideListenerFailed: The engine couldn't open its door — most often the port is already taken. Turn this off and on again, or pick another port under Advanced.
host.guideConfigInvalid: The saved settings didn't make sense, so nothing is served. Turn this off and on again to start clean.
host.guideGeneric: It's on, and something is in the way. Turning it off and on again usually clears it.
host.lanOptionWhy: Serves your mail to the ohmail app on your own network — no Tailscale needed for that. The connection is secured with a key this computer keeps, and the pairing code carries it, so the app knows it is really talking to this computer. A phone browser can't use it: a browser has no way to check that key.

host.lanNone: No usable network address was found on this computer.
host.lanListFailed: This computer's network addresses couldn't be read. Check again in a moment.
host.lanAloneWhy: You can still turn on same-network access: the ohmail app on your own network reaches your mail at this computer's address, secured by a key this computer keeps. Not for phone browsers — a browser needs the Tailscale address above.

host.lanFailed: The same-network door couldn't open — most often the port is already taken. Turn this off and on again, or pick another port under Advanced.
host.lanInvalid: The saved network address isn't usable anymore — this computer's address may have changed. Turn this off and on again and pick a current one.
host.lanBrowserNote: A phone browser can't use this address — it is secured with a key only the ohmail app can check, and a browser would warn instead. Browsers use the Tailscale address instead.
host.lanAddHint: You get a one-time pairing link to copy into an app or API client on your network. It works once and expires in five minutes.
host.lanMintedLead: Copy this pairing link into the app or API client on the other device. It pairs over your network in one step.

ai.title: AI proposes. You decide.
ai.body: Rules run first and do the bulk of the work with no AI at all — the design goal is that most of your mail is filed deterministically, by rules you can read and change. Where judgment actually helps, ohmail offers something: a door for a new sender, a draft in your voice, a nudge for a thread that went quiet. Every one of them waits for your yes, and nothing ever sends itself.
ai.status: The AI features run against a live model in production: the Screener proposes a door for a waiting sender, with a confidence and a reason, and the composer writes a first draft when you ask it for one. Both are proposals — they wait for your yes, nothing files or sends itself, and a pattern only begins running on its own once you have confirmed it often enough to graduate into a rule. The metering and spend limits that govern managed AI actions are in place and enforced: when the budget runs out the rules carry on, and nothing else changes.

ai.pointGrad: Decide the same way three times and ohmail asks to make it a rule. You approve it once — from then on it runs deterministically, with no AI at all.
ai.pointOtp: When mail carries a verification code or login link, that code is stripped before anything reaches AI, and the mail is never forwarded and never routed automatically — structurally, with no setting to turn it off. You always see the message in full; only what a model would read is stripped.
ai.pointByoTitle: Your key, your machine — or ours
ai.pointByo: On the desktop app your mail stays on your machine, with no ohmail server in the loop — and its AI, if you want one, is your own API key or a local model, set in the app; the bill is yours. On Cloud: a monthly bag of AI credits is included, and mail keeps flowing rules-only when it runs out.

On the desktop app your mail is already on your machine, so reading and searching work with the wifi off; in the browser that holds for the tab you have open, not for a cold start with no network.

get.sub: One product. Run it yourself for free — as a desktop app, or hosted on your own hardware — or let us run it for you. The code is public, licensed AGPL-3.0, and the hosted service is built from the same repository.
get.standaloneBody: The complete app on your machine: it connects to your own IMAP server and organizes your mailbox locally — no account, no ohmail server in the loop. macOS, Windows and Linux. Running it is already a self-hosted ohmail: the whole organizer, on hardware you own.

get.shDesktopBody: One switch in Settings → Devices, and your phone opens your mail through your own computer — over Tailscale, a private tunnel between your own devices, while it is awake. On a machine that stays awake, that is your own ohmail server, around the clock.

get.managedLead: Don't want to worry about hosting?

get.moveTitle: Your settings live in your mailbox, and move with it.
get.moveBody: The senders you've screened, your rules, your notification choices, your away reply and your tag names are stored in the mailbox itself — a few kilobytes of versioned JSON in a hidden folder. Pick any option above and change your mind later: connect the same mailbox elsewhere, and ohmail finds your settings and asks before using them. Leave ohmail entirely and those decisions are still yours, in your own mailbox, in a format anything can parse.

compare.title: Your mailbox, or theirs.
compare.sub: We like the apps that rethink mail — the ones that screen senders, the ones that add AI to your inbox. They pushed the craft forward and we admire the work. What we don't like is where the organization ends up: inside someone else's app, staying behind when you go. So this table is about one axis only — whose mailbox it is.
compare.openUs: AGPL-3.0 — the apps and the server behind ohmail.app, in one public repository. Only the hosted service's billing machinery is private.
compare.openOthers: Closed source as a rule; where an app is open, the service that organizes the mail is not.
compare.addressesUs: Stays exactly where it is — ohmail connects over IMAP
compare.addressesOthers: Either your mail moves into their service, or only a provider or two qualify
compare.foldersUs: Real IMAP folders on your server, readable by any client
compare.foldersOthers: In their apps and their cloud — not on your server
compare.settingsUs: Stored in the mailbox itself, as plain JSON in an open, published format — readable anytime, by anything, and they move with the mailbox
compare.settingsOthers: Kept in their service; no export includes them
compare.leaveUs: Your mailbox stays organized, and your rules travel with it — to a server you run, to the free desktop app, or to no ohmail at all
compare.leaveOthers: An export file at best; the organization stays behind
compare.desktopUs: A real mail client with the engine inside: your mail is on your own disk, so it opens, reads and searches with no network — and the standalone install organizes your mailbox from your machine
compare.desktopOthers: A desktop window around their web app — the organizing happens in their cloud, not on your machine
compare.aiUs: Optional and gated — AI proposes, you decide; only a pattern you have confirmed often enough runs on its own
compare.aiOthers: Built into their cloud — or missing entirely
compare.note: Compared as of August 2026, from each product's own published documentation.
compare.usLine: ohmail's answer to every row is the same answer: it's your mailbox. Several of them, in fact — ohmail organizes two, five, ten IMAP mailboxes at once, drafts replies in your voice, learns your decisions into rules you can read and change, and never asks you to change your address, your provider, or your other mail apps.
compare.goodwill: These are good products made by people who care about mail. The right model is the one that fits your life, and it may not be ours — that is a fine outcome. We only insist on one thing: the choice should stay yours, and so should the mailbox.

data.title: Where your mail lives.
data.sub: Three ways to run one product. The mailbox is the master in all of them; what differs is whose machine holds the working copy.
data.desktopRuns: Your machine. No account, no ohmail server in the loop — macOS, Windows and Linux.
data.desktopCopy: On your own disk, so it reads and searches with no network. It never leaves your machine.
data.desktopAi: Optional: your own key, or a local model.
data.selfRuns: A server you run — the same open server behind ohmail.app, from one compose file.
data.selfCopy: In a database on your box, where it powers search and sync to your devices.
data.selfAi: Optional: your own Anthropic API key. Without one, everything else works.
data.cloudRuns: Our EU servers — the same server, run for you, and awake when your devices are not.
data.cloudCopy: On EU servers, encrypted at rest, up to your plan's storage; past it, new mail is shown from your mailbox as a preview. Deleted with your account — from backups within 30 days.
data.cloudAi: Included in your plan and metered. When the credits run out, mail keeps flowing rules-only.
data.same: Cloud is self-hosting, done for you: the same open server, the same organizer, the same mailbox as the master. What changes is whose machine holds the copy — and that we bill for running it.
data.honest: The fine print for Cloud: it is not end-to-end encrypted. The service reads mail to file and search it, and a small number of people with production database access could technically read it. Never sold, never mined, never used for anything but serving you.
data.aiNote: AI on Cloud goes to Anthropic under commercial API terms: your mail is never used to train models, and requests are retained only briefly (currently up to 30 days); there is no zero-retention agreement yet. On every tier, a credential inside a message — a code, a login link, a reset token — is stripped before a request is built, and automatic routing skips that mail entirely. Structural, not a setting.

faq.title: Questions, answered.
faq.q1: What happens to my existing folders?
faq.a1: Nothing destructive. The folders you already have are left exactly as they are; ohmail organizes new mail into real IMAP folders on your server. Everything stays visible to any other mail client, on any device.
faq.a2: Anytime. Your mail never needs exporting — the originals live on your own server, in ordinary folders ohmail created in place, and nothing we do touches them. Be clear about what Cloud holds, though: a full copy of that mail — bodies, headers, subjects and senders — alongside your rules, tags and notes, because that is what makes search and push work. All of it is deleted with your account.
faq.a3: On Cloud: via the Claude API (Anthropic), under commercial API terms and within your plan's credits — the model runs at Anthropic, not on our servers. On the desktop app: wherever you point it — your own API key, or a local model through Ollama so nothing leaves your machine — set in the app, and off until you configure it. On a server you run: your own Anthropic API key today; a local-model option there is not built yet, and without a key everything else works. Either way, rules with no AI at all run first and are meant to handle most mail — and you can switch the AI off entirely without losing a single feature that files your mail.
faq.a4: The unit your plan is measured in. Actions cost what they cost us: screening a new sender or filing a message is 1 credit, a drafted reply is 15, a workflow proposal 20. Drafting reads a whole thread and writes prose, so it costs more than sorting one message — pricing them the same would only mean charging everybody for the expensive one. When the monthly budget runs out, mail keeps flowing rules-only until the next cycle. There are no overage charges — ever.
faq.a5: Not as a matter of practice, and our admin tools do not display message content — every response the console can produce is checked by a test that writes a marker into every text column of every table and fails if any of it reaches a staff response. The database itself does not yet refuse those columns to staff tooling: the column-restricted role that would enforce this below the application is built and tested but not yet live, and we will not claim it until it is. The honest fine print: Cloud mail is stored unencrypted at the application level and is not end-to-end encrypted, so someone with production database access could technically read it; that access is held by very few people, and the product privacy policy will spell out who and under what conditions when it publishes, before the first real mailbox connects. On Desktop the question doesn't arise — your mail never reaches our servers at all: the app runs as a real mail client against your own server, on macOS, Windows and Linux alike. Separately, nobody else gets to watch you read either: a spy pixel is blocked by default, so it cannot report that you opened anything — loading them is a choice you would have to make in Settings — and ohmail records who tried. Ordinary pictures do load, through our own proxy, which means the sender's server sees us and never your address.
faq.a6: Any IMAP mailbox: your own domain at Metanet or Infomaniak, iCloud, Gmail, Outlook, a self-hosted server. If it speaks IMAP, ohmail organizes it in place. Native Exchange sync over Microsoft Graph is on the roadmap; Microsoft 365 connects over IMAP, like every other mailbox here.
faq.q7: Is there a trial for Cloud?
faq.a7: Yes — 14 days, no card. It is the whole product: rules, sync, push and the web app all run, and it comes with 500 AI actions so the drafts and the Screener's suggestions are yours to try. Spend those and mail keeps flowing rules-only; the monthly allowance begins when a subscription does. Desktop needs no trial at all; it is free.
faq.q8: Desktop or Cloud — what’s the real difference?
faq.a8: The same model, the same vocabulary, and deliberately not the same privacy posture — that is the honest difference. Desktop is free and fully standalone: all processing local, no account, no artificial limits. It is a real mail client on all three platforms — it connects to your own IMAP server and organizes your mailbox on your machine, and because your mail is on your own disk it is there to read with the network down. Its AI, if you want one, is your own API key or a local model through Ollama — set in the app, off until you configure it. Cloud adds the web app, push notifications, always-on processing while your computer sleeps, and AI included from $9 a month — and it holds a copy of your mail on our servers to do that. The same download does either one; which door you take is a choice inside the app. Both are open today.

siteScreener.title: You decide who gets in.
siteScreener.body: The first time someone writes to you, they wait at the Screener — not in your inbox. One click picks the door, once, for every mail that sender ever writes: Ohbox for people, Reads for newsletters, Receipts for the paperwork. Or never again — which also unsubscribes you, where the list offers one click. Spam is one press too: the message moves to your mail server's own Junk folder, and that sender never asks again. Want help deciding? Switch on suggestions and ohmail proposes a door for each new sender as their mail arrives, at a price you see up front; plain newsletters and receipts it can file by itself, and a pattern you have confirmed often enough runs without asking — spam included. It deletes nothing on its own.

mailboxes.organizeHereQueuedLegacy: Asked for. Quit and reopen ohmail to organize this mailbox from this computer. If the other install is still running and renews its claim first, it keeps the mailbox and this one stays stood down.
mailboxes.organizeHereQueuedBlocked: Asked for — but {name} keeps this mailbox for as long as it is still checking in, whatever was asked for here. Stop it organizing there, then ask again.
mailboxes.setupAgainWhy: Walks through what ohmail files, how far back it screens, and AI — with what is set now filled in. Nothing moves until you agree.

onboarding.cancelWhat: Setup closes and the app opens as it is now. Nothing is half-applied: what you agreed to stays agreed, what you did not stays off. You can run setup again from Settings → Mailboxes.
onboarding.restartWhat: Back to the first step. Keep the mailbox you connected?
onboarding.welcomeTitle: ohmail holds first-time senders until you decide, and files everything else into folders in your own mailbox.
onboarding.welcomeLead: Setup takes a few minutes. Nothing moves until you say so.
onboarding.welcomeCloudTitle: Your email is confirmed. Now the mailbox ohmail will organize.
onboarding.mailboxLead: The mailbox ohmail organizes, in place. Real folders on your real server; your other mail apps keep seeing everything.
onboarding.passwordHint: Sealed on this computer and sent only to your mail server. Never your account password where the provider offers app passwords.
onboarding.passwordHintCloud: Sent to ohmail's server and stored sealed there; used only to reach this mailbox. Revocable at your provider at any time.
onboarding.user: Username, if it is not the address
onboarding.probeOk: {host} answered. Signed in as {user} · {count, plural, one {1 folder} other {# folders}}.
onboarding.probeOkDetail: Nothing has been read or moved. Continue to say what ohmail may do here.
onboarding.elsewhereLead: This mailbox already has an organizer. Two installs never organize one mailbox at once.
onboarding.elsewhereChoiceHereWhy: This install takes over on its next pass; {name} becomes a reader — it keeps its copy of your mail and stops moving anything.
onboarding.elsewhereChoiceReadWhy: This install reads, searches and sends. {name} keeps organizing. You can take over later from Settings → Mailboxes.
onboarding.elsewhereQueued: Asked for. This install takes over on its next pass — within a minute. Continue meanwhile.
onboarding.consentTitle: What ohmail will do to this mailbox
onboarding.consentBody: ohmail re-arranges your existing inbox into folders it creates in your mailbox: Ohbox, Reads, Receipts, Screener, Screened and Quarantine. They are ordinary IMAP folders — every other mail client sees them too, and you can leave any time with your mail exactly where it is.
onboarding.consentHistory: Mail older than the window you choose next stays in the Inbox and is listed under History. History is a view: nothing in it moves.
onboarding.consentNothingYet: Nothing moves until you agree on the next screen.
onboarding.windowTitle: How far back should ohmail screen?
onboarding.windowLead: Senders with mail inside the window go through the Screener. Older mail stays in the Inbox and is listed under History — kept, searchable, not screened.
onboarding.winAllWhy: Every sender goes through the Screener. Nothing is listed under History unscreened.
onboarding.windowLater: You can widen this later in Settings → Screener: older senders then wait in the Screener as undecided, and a decision moves that sender's mail.
onboarding.windowGone: That mailbox is no longer connected, so nothing was saved. Close setup, connect it again, and run setup from there.
onboarding.aiLead: A model can suggest where a first-time sender belongs and draft replies. Without one, rules do all the filing — that is a complete way to run ohmail.
onboarding.aiYesWhy: You choose where the model runs on the next screen.
onboarding.aiNoWhy: Rules only. You can turn this on later in Settings.
onboarding.aiYesCloudWhy: Runs on ohmail's servers, inside your plan's AI credits. When they run out, rules carry on.
onboarding.aiYesSelfhostWhy: Runs on this server with the operator's Anthropic key.
onboarding.providerCloudBody: Suggestions and drafts run on ohmail's servers through the Claude API, inside your plan's AI credits. Only the sender, the subject and a short extract are sent. Mail ohmail judges sensitive is never sent.
onboarding.providerSelfhostOn: The operator has set an Anthropic key on this server. Suggestions and drafts run through it.
onboarding.providerSelfhostOff: This server has no AI key set. Rules do all the filing; the operator can add a key later.
onboarding.pullLead: ohmail is reading the mailbox and filing what falls inside the window. You can leave this screen — the status bar carries these counters.
onboarding.etaSoon: Working out how long this takes…
onboarding.eta: About {eta} left · {rate, number} messages a minute
onboarding.etaDone: Done. {screened, number} screened, {history, number} listed under History.
onboarding.pullResumed: The connection dropped and came back. The pull continues where it stopped.
onboarding.decideLead: One sender is waiting. Where should their mail go? The decision becomes a rule for their future mail; the ✓ half also marks the waiting mail read.
onboarding.decideReads: Reads — newsletters, things to read later
onboarding.decideScreened: Screen out — filed away; their future mail follows without asking
onboarding.decideAfter: Then the Screener proper: every other waiting sender, the same three verbs.
onboarding.doneScreened: {count, plural, one {1 message} other {# messages}} screened
onboarding.doneScreenedWhy: Each decision is a rule under Settings → Rules.
onboarding.doneHistoryWhy: Older than the window. Still in the Inbox — nothing there moved.
onboarding.doneWhere: Ohbox, Reads, Receipts, Screener, Screened, Quarantine — in your mailbox, next to your Inbox.
onboarding.doneSettings: Everything here can be changed under Settings — and setup can be run again from Settings → Mailboxes.
onboarding.doneReaderReadsWhy: Reading, searching, marking read and sending all work. It moves nothing and screens nothing — the organizer below does that.
onboarding.doneReaderClaim: You can organize from here later
onboarding.doneReaderClaimWhy: Settings → Mailboxes has the button. Stop the organizer where it runs first, or it keeps the mailbox.
onboarding.pairLead: Scan with the phone's camera. It opens ohmail there and pairs in one step — the code works once and expires in five minutes.
onboarding.pairSameNetworkWhy: The phone reaches this computer over your own network. Off, it also works over Tailscale.
onboarding.phoneWelcome: Scan the code ohmail shows under Settings → Devices, on your computer or on the web.
onboarding.phoneBannerWhy: This phone reads the mailbox. Decisions are made where it is organized.
